# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–26 (Complete – Updated 189)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Summer-to-autumn of seventh year, transitioning to new era**. John Sedley deceased (died peacefully in sleep; buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife). Mr. Osborne deceased (died four days after stroke; found at foot of dressing-table). Major Dobbin appointed executor of Osborne's will. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established as heir. **Now on summer tour voyage**: Amelia, Georgy, Jos, and Major Dobbin embarking on ship for travel.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 26 opens "summer of seventh year," extends through autumn, now includes ship departure for summer tour.
- **Major locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre, Gillespie Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Piccadilly; Madras; St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John); Bengal; Salford; Regent's Park; Richmond (Star and Garter); Gulton; Harrowgate; Hill farms; Roehampton; Hampton Court; Staveton (harbor town); Calcutta; Jamaica; ship at anchor.

## John Sedley's Final Illness and Death (Chapter 26)
**Nursing and Reconciliation**: Amelia nursed father devotedly during final illness; her "sole business of her life" to tend him. Old Sedley, "touched by her love and goodness," forgave past grievances he and wife had debated. One night made confession: "Oh, Emmy, I've been thinking we were very unkind and unjust to you." Amelia knelt and prayed by his bedside.

**Death**: Died peacefully in sleep. Buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife. Major Dobbin, Jos, and Georgy followed remains to grave in black cloth coach. Jos returned to Star and Garter at Richmond after event. Amelia remained, "bowed down by no especial grief," prayed for calm, painless death like father's, thought of his faith and resignation.

## Mr. Osborne's Stroke and Death (Chapter 26)
**Mental Change**: Osborne's mind visibly changing. Asked Georgy about his uncle Jos; laughed at boy's imitations. Told Miss Osborne to leave card upon Sedley—"There's no quarrel betwigst me and him anyhow."

**Reconciliation Dinner**: Card returned; Jos and Dobbin invited to "most splendid and stupid" dinner. Every inch of family plate exhibited; best company asked. Sedley took down Miss O. to dinner; she was gracious to him. Dobbin sat apart, timid, by Osborne's side. Jos praised turtle soup, asked about Madeira.

**Dobbin's Advocacy**: Osborne asked Major repeatedly about Mrs. George Osborne. Dobbin spoke eloquently of her sufferings, passionate attachment to husband's memory, tender duty to parents, sacrifice of boy. Told Osborne: "You don't know what she endured, sir...If she took your son away from you, she gave hers to you; and however much you loved your George, depend on it, she loved hers ten times more." Osborne replied: "By God, you are a good feller, sir."

**Reconciliation Planned**: Osborne had never considered widow felt pain at parting from boy or that his fortune could grieve her. Reconciliation was "announced as speedy and inevitable"; Amelia's "heart already began to beat at the notion of the awful meeting."

**Prevention by Death**: Meeting never took place. Old Sedley's lingering illness and death intervened. Osborne "much shaken of late, and aged, and his mind was working inwardly." Had sent for lawyers; "probably changed something in his will." Medical man found him "shaky, agitated"; prescribed blood-letting and seaside, neither taken.

**Stroke and Final Days**: Found in dressing-room at foot of dressing-table in fit. Doctors sent; Georgy stayed from school; bleeders and cuppers came. Osborne partially regained consciousness but never spoke again, "though he tried dreadfully once or twice." Died in four days. Shutters closed toward Russell Square garden. Undertaker's men came; Bullock rushed from City, anxiously asking: "How much money had he left to that boy? Not half, surely?"

**Last Moments**: Pocket of dressing-gown contained letter with great red seal George had written from Waterloo. Key to box containing son's papers also in pocket; seals and envelopes broken—likely night before seizure when butler found him reading great red family Bible in study.

## Mr. Osborne's Will (Chapter 26)
**Terms**: Half property left to George Osborne (minor); remainder between two sisters. Mr. Bullock to continue commercial house affairs for joint benefit or exit as he thought fit. **Annuity**: Five hundred pounds, chargeable on George's property, left to Amelia, "the widow of my beloved son, George Osborne," who was to resume guardianship of boy.

**Dobbin's Provision**: Major William Dobbin appointed executor, named "my beloved son's friend." Will stated: "as out of his kindness and bounty, and with his own private funds, he maintained my grandson and my son's widow, when they were otherwise without means of support...I hereby thank him heartily for his love and regard for them, and beseech him to accept such a sum as may be sufficient to purchase his commission as a Lieutenant-Colonel, or to be disposed of in any way he may think fit."

**Osborne's Intent**: Will showed "the hatred which he had so long cherished had gone out of his heart." Narrator hopes old man tried to say he wanted to see Amelia and be reconciled before leaving world—"most likely that."

## Amelia's Transformation and New Life (Chapter 26)
**Upon Learning of Reconciliation**: When heard father-in-law reconciled to her, heart melted; grateful for fortune left. When learned Georgy restored to her and discovered William's bounty supported her in poverty, that William gave her husband and son—"oh, then she sank on her knees, and prayed for blessings on that constant and kind heart; she bowed down and humbled herself, and kissed the feet, as it were, of that beautiful and generous affection."

**Visiting Gaunt House**: Clad in deep sables (mourning), visited deserted mansion not entered since girlhood. Found straw littered in front where vans had been laden. Entered great blank rooms bearing marks where pictures and mirrors hung. Went up great blank stone staircases into upper rooms—where grandpapa died, as Georgy whispered—then higher into George's own room. Boy clung to her side; she thought of another besides him—his father. Knew it had been his father's room as well as his own.

**Window Reflection and Memory**: At open window (where she once gazed with sick heart when child first taken from her), looked out over trees of Russell Square toward old house where she was born and passed many happy days of sacred youth. "They all came back to her, the pleasant holidays, the kind faces, the careless, joyful past times, and the long pains and trials that had since cast her down." She thought of man who had been her "constant protector, her good genius, her sole benefactor, her tender and generous friend."

**New Household at Richmond**: Took temporary house at Richmond. Lawyers visited frequently (and noted visit in bill). Major Dobbin had room there, rode over frequently on business behalf of his little ward. "Very silent as they drove back to Richmond."

## Reconciliation with Mrs. Frederick Bullock (Chapter 26)
**Bullock's Change of Heart**: Mrs. Frederick Bullock (female Bullock, aunt of Georgy), "although despoiled by that little monster of one-half of the sum which she expected from her father, nevertheless showed her charitableness of spirit by being reconciled to the mother and the boy."

**Visit to Richmond**: Roehampton not far from Richmond. One day chariot with golden bullocks emblazoned on panels and "flaccid children within" drove to Amelia's house. Bullock family "made an irruption into the garden, where Amelia was reading a book, Jos was in an arbour placidly dipping strawberries into wine, and the Major in one of his Indian jackets was giving a back to Georgy, who chose to jump over him." Georgy went over his head and bounded into advance of Bullocks, "with immense black bows in their hats, and huge black sashes, accompanying their mourning mamma."

**Reunion**: "Those ladies accordingly met, after an absence of more than fifteen years. During Emmy's cares and poverty the other had never once thought about coming to see her, but now that she was decently prosperous in the world, her sister-in-law came to her as a matter of course."

**Bullock's Scheming (rumor)**: Per Rowdy and Hollyock's conversation as they drove away: Mrs. Bullock "is always scheming and managing. She wants Mrs. Osborne's account to be taken from our house to hers--and the way in which she coaxes that boy and makes him sit by that blear-eyed little Rosa is perfectly ridiculous."

## Miss Swartz's Renewed Friendship (Chapter 26)
"Numbers more" visited newly prosperous Amelia. Old friend Miss Swartz and her husband came "thundering over from Hampton Court, with flaming yellow liveries, and was as impetuously fond of Amelia as ever. Miss Swartz would have liked her always if she could have seen her. One must do her that justice. But, que voulez vous?--in this vast town one has not the time to go and seek one's friends; if they drop out of the rank they disappear, and we march on without them. Who is ever missed in Vanity Fair?"

## Georgy Osborne (Chapter 26)
**Character Continuation**: Still superior, commanding figure. Now eleven years old; boy's "quick brain" revealed grandfather "a dullard." Day boy at Reverend Lawrence Veal's School (Hart Street, Bloomsbury). Marked aristos in Greek, optimus in Latin, très bien in French. Schoolboys call Veal "Longtail"—name Georgy gave him.

**Friendships**: Young Todd of Coram Street greatest friend. Both attended principal theatres. **Mrs. Todd's plan (rumor)**: Privately wondered if Georgy and daughter Rosa Jemima "might happen."

**Mockery of Relations**: Told stories at night to mother about relatives. When Dobbin dropped in after Georgy praised him to old Osborne, boy increased confusion by telling Dobbin: "I say, Dob, there's such an uncommon nice girl wants to marry you...It's Aunt O....And I say, Dob, how prime it would be to have you for my uncle." Old Sedley's call from next room ended laughter.

**Inheritance**: Now heir to half Osborne's substantial property. Will restored him to mother's guardianship. Boy remained active, imperious, good-natured presence.

**On Summer Tour**: Young imperious gentleman aboard ship, "our young friend George Osborne," gobbling biscuits (having breakfasted at Richmond full three hours before). Aboard with mother, Uncle Jos, and a gentleman (Major Dobbin) "of whom they used to see a good deal," the four "about to make a summer tour."

## Summer Tour Voyage (Chapter 26)
**Ship Departure**: Aboard ship at Staveton harbor town. Passengers' carriages being loaded. Kirsch (courier/interpreter) bellowing polyglot instructions to ship's men on luggage. Kirsch informed other couriers and Hebrew gentlemen (who speculated on finances) that carriage belonged to "a Nabob from Calcutta and Jamaica enormously rich" with whom he was engaged to travel. Young Georgy clambered over carriages and imperials to reach his own carriage, descended through window with couriers' applause.

**Jos on Deck**: Jos seated on deck under awning, "pretty nearly opposite to the Earl of Bareacres and his family, whose proceedings absorbed the Bengalee almost entirely." Both noble couple "looked rather younger than in the eventful year '15, when Jos remembered to have seen them at Brussels (indeed, he always gave out in India that he was intimately acquainted with them)." Lady Bareacres' hair, formerly dark, now "a beautiful golden auburn"; Lord Bareacres' whiskers, formerly red, now "of a rich black with purple and green reflections in the light." "But changed as they were, the movements of the noble pair occupied Jos's mind entirely. The presence of a Lord fascinated him, and he could look at nothing else."

**Jos's Traveller's Bravado and Seasickness**: When asked if weather would cause concern, Jos waved hand scornfully: "If you had made the voyages we have, you wouldn't much care about the weather." Nevertheless, "traveller as he was, he passed the night direfully sick in his carriage, where his courier tended him with brandy-and-water and every luxury."

## Major Dobbin (Chapter 24–26)
[Summary retained from previous: Return, reunion with Amelia, declaration and refusal, discovery of support, reconciliation with Osborne, advocacy, executor status—all as previously detailed.]

## Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 23–24)
Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand per year. Complete moral transformation: maintains honor, fulfills obligations, provides for son's education, compensates those wronged. Separated from Rebecca permanently after duel with Steyne.

## Rebecca's Fate (Chapter 24)
Bailiffs seized Curzon Street property. Rawdon made her "tolerable annuity." Whereabouts unknown; "Who cared!"
